headline: Decide where a certificate-transparency request goes and which trust anchors it is made under before reading anything else the caller passed, and keep a copied byte argument out of the caller's reach.
summary: Reading a value out of a caller's object can run the caller's own code, and a certificate-transparency verb reads its own options first: the fields of a signed tree head, the elements of a certificate chain. A getter on one of those ran before the request had been shaped, so it could still choose the host the request went to, or empty the list of trust anchors the connection was pinned to. The anchor case left the URL correct, so nothing about the request looked wrong. Each verb now settles its transport, its URL and its TLS configuration at its entry, before it reads any other value it was given, and the trust material is copied there rather than referenced. The copy itself needed fixing too, in every verb in the package rather than only these: it was taken out of a shared allocation pool, which left it reachable from a caller whose own value came from that pool, and a key copied that way could be rewritten after the verb had taken it.

Fixed: `pki.ct.getProofByHash` and `pki.ct.getSthConsistency` read the fields of the signed tree heads they were given before the request was shaped, and `pki.ct.addChain` and `pki.ct.addPreChain` read the elements of the certificate chain. A getter on any of those fields runs the caller's code at that moment, so it could rewrite the URL and send the request to another host, or empty `tls.anchors` after the check that refuses an unpinned log had already approved them, which opened the connection with no anchors at all while leaving the URL it reported unchanged. `pki.ct.fetchLogList` had the same ordering for a different reason: it parsed the URL, which converts it and so can run a caller's `toString`, before it read the TLS configuration. No order of reads fixes this on its own, because whichever option is read first, reading a value nested inside it runs the caller's code and that code can rewrite the ones not yet read: reading the TLS first lets a getter on `tls.anchors` rewrite the URL and the pinned key, and shaping the request first lets a header getter replace the key a tree head is verified under, in place if it is a buffer. So two shapes are refused rather than ordered around. `opts.url` has to be a string, because asking an object for its text form runs the caller's code, and so does `opts.sigUrl`, the detached-signature URL `pki.ct.fetchLogList` takes, which is a destination on the same footing. `opts.tls` may not carry an accessor, because reading its members has to be inert. All three draw `ct/bad-input`. With those refused, every option a verb declares is taken at its entry, the pinned key is copied there, and the request is sent and the signature checked from what was taken. A caller passing plain values and a string URL sees no change, and options supplied through a defaults object on the prototype chain still work, including the transport.

The trust anchors, the client certificate and the client key a `pki.ct` verb is given are copied where they are taken, not referenced. Copying the anchor list copied the references in it, and an anchor is a mutable buffer, so a getter elsewhere in the options could write other bytes over an anchor after the check that refuses an unpinned log had approved it: every reference still pointed where it had, the URL was unchanged, and the connection was made under trust material no check had seen. A PEM string cannot be altered after the fact and is taken as it is; a value that is neither bytes nor a string reaches the transport unchanged, so a shape it does not accept still draws the refusal it draws today. Two side effects of taking the copy: a byte source that is not a Buffer, such as the `ArrayBuffer` that `crypto.subtle.exportKey` returns, is normalized to one and now reaches the connection as a usable anchor, and an anchor larger than the DER ceiling is refused as `ct/too-large` where it was previously passed on.

A TLS setting nobody set can no longer be answered by `Object.prototype`. A verb that fetches builds a record of the TLS settings for the request, and where the caller named none that record was an empty object literal, which inherits. A value installed on `Object.prototype` was therefore read from it, and one of the settings read that way is `useSystemStore`, the opt-in that turns off the refusal of a server with no pinned trust anchor: with it installed, a call that had named neither a transport nor an anchor opened a connection trusting the system store where it should have been refused. The record now has no prototype, so nothing can be inherited into it. Fixed in `pki.ct`, `pki.acme`, `pki.est`, `pki.scep`, `pki.cmp`, the certificate-path builder's authority-information-access fetch, and `pki.transport` itself, which is the refusal every one of those delegates to.

A byte input copied at a verb's entry is copied into storage of its own. The copy was taken with `Buffer.from`, which for a small result allocates out of the shared 64 KiB pool, so a caller whose own value came from that pool holds a view of the whole store and the copy lands inside it at another offset. A caller's code running after the copy and before the copy is used could then find it and overwrite it: supplying the pinned log key as a pooled buffer and rewriting the copy from inside the transport had `pki.ct.getSth` accept a tree head signed by another key. This is the copy every verb in the package takes of a byte argument, so the fix reaches each of them, not only the certificate-transparency ones. Copies of a caller's keys, hashes and signed bytes are now out of the caller's reach once taken, which is what taking them is for.

A request URL is parsed with the `URL` constructor and the string conversion the package captured at load, in every module that builds a destination from one: `pki.ct`, `pki.acme`, `pki.est`, `pki.scep`, `pki.cmp`, `pki.ocsp`, the revocation fetcher, the path validator, the HTTP transport and its Digest authentication. Reading either off the global object at the moment of the parse read whatever had been installed there by then. A caller's code running mid-request, through a getter on an option the verb had yet to read, could replace the constructor with one answering a genuine URL that named another host, or replace the conversion so it answered with another host's URL outright, and the endpoint was built from that answer while the URL the caller passed was still the one the call reported. Capturing the constructor is not enough on its own, because the value it returns reads its parts through `URL.prototype`, which is also replaceable: redefining `href` there answered every read of the destination. So `pki.ct` and the HTTP transport read each part of a parsed destination, the scheme, host, port, path and query, through accessors captured at load, and the transport reads the scheme once and decides from that one string whether the request is allowed, whether a trust anchor is required and which port it defaults to.
